questions.q: For the lab's planned real-hardware run (p=4 layers, 8 parameters, 150 iterations, 4096 shots/evaluation, parameter-shift rule), what is the total projected shot budget?
options: 16,384 shots
2,400 shots
614,400 shots
questions.explain: evals_per_gradient = 8*2=16; total_executions = 16*150=2400; total_shots = 2400*4096 = 9,830,400 -- verified by direct computation, far more than '4096 shots, one circuit' would suggest.

questions.q: Given a real-hardware allocation budget of 2,000,000 shots, how does the projected 9,830,400-shot plan compare, and what does the lab say this requires?
options: It's within budget, so no changes are needed
It's roughly 5x over budget, requiring a concrete adjustment with a calculated trade-off, not a vague 'be more efficient' plan
It's exactly at budget
Shot budgets don't need to be compared against allocations
questions.explain: 9.8 million projected shots against a 2 million budget is roughly a 5x overage. The lab insists any fix be a concrete, calculable adjustment (fewer iterations, fewer shots, or a different split between simulator and hardware), not a vague intention.

questions.q: Why does reducing shots per evaluation from 4096 to 2048 carry a real trade-off, according to the lab?
options: It has no trade-off at all and is a free win
Per Lesson 7, halving shots roughly doubles the standard error on each gradient evaluation, which can make the optimizer's gradient estimates noisier and potentially destabilize convergence
It doubles the circuit depth automatically
It makes the circuit require more qubits
questions.explain: Standard error scales as 1/sqrt(n) (Lesson 7), so halving shots increases noise in each gradient estimate -- a real cost to convergence quality, not a free reduction in cost.

questions.q: What is the lab's recommended adjustment that avoids trading away either convergence quality or statistical precision?
options: Cut optimizer iterations to 1
Run the full iterative optimization on a local simulator (cheap, fast, no hardware-queue cost), then submit only the final converged parameters to real hardware for a validation run
Submit every iteration to real hardware regardless of cost
Increase shots per evaluation to reduce noise
questions.explain: Training on a simulator (shown cheap and fast in Step 1's profiling) and reserving real hardware only for a final validation run brings real-hardware shot cost down to a single evaluation's worth of shots, avoiding the convergence or precision trade-offs of the other two options.

questions.q: After switching to train-on-simulator/validate-on-hardware with one final 4096-shot evaluation, how does the real-hardware shot cost compare to the 2,000,000-shot budget?
options: It exceeds the budget by 5x, same as before
It is exactly at the budget limit
It is comfortably within budget by several orders of magnitude (4,096 shots vs. a 2,000,000-shot allocation)
It cannot be calculated without running the experiment first
questions.explain: Reserving hardware for just one final validation evaluation brings the real-hardware cost down to 4,096 shots total -- several orders of magnitude under the 2,000,000-shot budget, while the simulator-side training costs no hardware-queue budget at all.
